summary.text: Polar night happens inside the polar circles when the Sun stays below the horizon for more than 24 hours.
It lasts from 24 hours just inside the polar circles up to 179 days at the poles, and it is night in one polar region while it is day in the other.
In most cases polar night is not full darkness: sunlight bent over the horizon gives a midday twilight whose brightness depends on latitude.

items.explain: Polar night lengthens with latitude, from 24 hours just inside the polar circles to 179 days at the poles.

paragraphs.heading: What polar night is
paragraphs.text: Polar night is when the Sun stays below the horizon for more than 24 hours, something that happens only inside the polar circles. Its opposite, when the Sun stays up for more than 24 hours, is called polar day or the midnight sun. The two poles take turns: while the Arctic Circle has its day, the Antarctic Circle has its night, and the other way round. How long it lasts depends on latitude: a single day of 24 hours just within the circles, rising to 179 days at the poles themselves.

paragraphs.heading: Shades of twilight
paragraphs.text: Twilight is the slow change into and out of darkness while the Sun is below the horizon, and it can be defined in several ways. Civil twilight runs while the Sun is 0 to 6 degrees down, and bright objects such as Venus and the star Sirius can be seen. Nautical twilight lasts until 12 degrees, with the horizon still clear enough to navigate by. Astronomical twilight goes on to 18 degrees; past that, no bent sunlight can be seen, and true night begins.

paragraphs.heading: Not total darkness
paragraphs.text: A place in polar night is usually not fully dark. Sunlight bends over the horizon, so most of the time such a place is in one of the stages of polar twilight, each matched to one kind of ordinary twilight. As in places with daylight, midday is normally the brightest time. The same bending of light makes polar day last longer than polar night and cover a slightly larger area.

paragraphs.heading: Civil polar twilight
paragraphs.text: Between roughly 67° 24' and 72° 34' of latitude, the Sun stays down all day at the winter solstice, and noon brings only civil twilight, never true daylight. Light scattered and bent by the upper atmosphere still gives enough light at midday for most normal outdoor activities. Under thick cloud, though, places such as the coast of Finnmark in Norway get an unusually dark day. Street lamps may then stay on at noon, and outdoor light can be dimmer than in many lit rooms.

paragraphs.heading: Darker further north
paragraphs.text: Between about 72° 34' and 78° 34', midday brings only nautical twilight: you can make out the rough shapes of things on the ground, but not do detailed work outside. Longyearbyen, on Svalbard, has this from about 11 November until 30 January. Between about 78° 34' and 84° 34', midday brings only astronomical twilight, and the sky is dark enough at noon to observe stars, except where light pollution, moonlight or auroras brighten it. Alert, in Nunavut, the northernmost settlement in the world, has this from roughly November 19 to January 22.

paragraphs.heading: Light and mood
paragraphs.text: People with seasonal affective disorder often turn to therapy with artificial light. The mental benefits of daylight need high light levels, up to 10,000 lux, which no stage of twilight provides. So for them, the midday twilight anywhere inside the polar circles still counts as polar night.
